title: When a No-Brainer Becomes a Deal-Breaker
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos argues that the alphabetic principle is the non-negotiable starting point for beginning readers, and that the Structured Word Inquiry community weakens its case by selectively citing researchers such as Ehri, Share and Apel. She anchors the piece in a SPELLTalk discussion, quoting Ehri and Apel to show that letter-sound knowledge comes first and that morphology is layered on top, with attention to cognitive load. She also gives space to a first-grade teacher, William Feerick, who proposes framing early instruction around morphemes, and treats his ideas respectfully while noting that classroom materials constrain him. Her move is to separate what is important from what must come first: prioritization is not exclusion, and morphology instruction need not displace phonics. She concludes that a morphocentric curriculum for beginners is a deal-breaker absent compelling research, invoking Hendrick's warning against stories that are beautiful and deserve to be true.
points: The alphabetic principle explains how speech maps onto print while morphology explains how print encodes meaning, so the two are complementary rather than competing.
Janetos accuses SWI advocates of cherry-picking researchers (Ehri on morphology, Share on combinatoriality, Apel on morphological awareness) while ignoring their support for early phonics.
Apel's cognitive-load advice, to make learning abnormally easy by targeting only one metalinguistic skill per lesson, is offered as a practical check on stacking morphology onto phonics.
The real question is not whether morphology matters but how and when to teach each linguistic component, and orthographic mapping is her North Star for sequencing.
She names the demotion of the alphabetic principle the authenticity illusion, a belief that the truth of the writing system outranks how beginners are best taught.
quotes: Teaching the alphabetic principle is fundamental and gets the ball rolling. To draw attention to plural suffixes, students need to know the shape of the letter S, named “ess” and that it can represent /s/ or /z/. They need to know the other letter-sounds that spell the base words. Hence, knowledge of letters, their shapes, names and sounds and how they are applied to read words comes first.

Whether we are teaching the monomorphemic word jet or the bound morpheme ject, our students need to decode it before accessing its meaning. If we don’t teach those sound-symbol connections, we are asking our most vulnerable learners to jump over unnecessary hurdles to get to word recognition. This is our North Star: facilitating orthographic mapping.

We MUST be aware of the “learning load” any one lesson places on the student. I always said to my grad students: “Make learning abnormally easy.” So, when engaged in instruction, we do the best we can to make everything in the lesson known but the one goal we have in mind to help the student learn the new information (ZPD [Zone of Proximal Development]). That then translates to, in any one lesson, only focusing on PA [Phonemic Awareness], MA [Morphological Awareness], or OK [Orthographic Knowledge] – we don’t tackle more than one metalinguistic skill at a time.

The fact that a concept is part of a larger system does not make it invalid; it makes it foundational—or fundamental—to return to Linnea Ehri’s explanation. Adherence to the alphabetic principle does not preclude acknowledging the importance of morphology—it is simply a concept we apply to teach monomorphemic words to beginning readers. This principle may not explain our entire writing system, but it explains enough of it to give our students escape velocity to explore the universe of our morphology-rich language.

Asking students to decode CVC words at the beginning does not doom them to a lifetime of morphology-free literacy. This failure to distinguish between the requirements of literacy components—what, when, and how to teach them—reflects the everything, everywhere, all at once approach, which leads me to ask: When did prioritization become synonymous with exclusion?

Those of us who appreciate and accept the alphabetic principle—its implications for instruction as well as its limitations—cannot abandon it without strong evidence. To dispense with what is essential for beginning readers and relegate this principle to a supporting role by adopting a morphocentric curriculum is a deal-breaker: no deal until there is compelling research recommending it.
